decks.domain: Missouri sharing the road: motorcycles, large trucks, pedestrians, bicycles, mopeds, electric bicycles, funeral processions, road rage, drunk drivers and littering

cards.front: Why are motorcycles involved in crashes with drivers who did not notice them?
cards.back: Drivers often fail to notice motorcycles, and judging how fast or how far away a motorcycle is can be hard.

cards.front: Why should a motorcycle rider not count on having the right-of-way at intersections?
cards.back: At intersections a motorcycle rider should not count on having the right-of-way, because drivers may not see the bike or may think it is moving slower than it is.

cards.front: May you share a lane with a motorcycle?
cards.back: Never share a lane with a motorcycle, because the rider needs the whole lane to stay safe.

cards.front: How much room do you give a motorcycle when passing it?
cards.back: When passing a motorcycle, give it a full lane width instead of squeezing by, and wait for a clear stretch if the lane is too narrow to share.

cards.front: Why might a motorcycle ahead suddenly change speed or lane position?
cards.back: Riders shift speed and lane position for manhole covers, diagonal rail tracks, debris or strong wind, so be ready to react when you follow one.

cards.front: What does Missouri law require motorcycle riders to wear?
cards.back: Missouri law requires motorcycle riders to wear a helmet.

cards.front: What license is needed to ride a motorcycle on public streets?
cards.back: Riding a motorcycle on public streets requires a valid driver license with a motorcycle endorsement, or a motorcycle license.

cards.front: How can motorcycle riders make themselves easier to see?
cards.back: Motorcycle riders should wear bright clothing, stay out of blind spots, use proper lights and reflectors at night, and signal and scan before slowing, merging or turning.

decks.domain: Missouri sharing the road: motorcycles, large trucks, pedestrians, bicycles, mopeds, electric bicycles, funeral processions, road rage, drunk drivers and littering

cards.front: How heavy and how long can a typical tractor-trailer be?
cards.back: A typical tractor-trailer can weigh as much as eighty thousand pounds, and with a long trailer the whole rig can be longer than ninety feet.

cards.front: How long can double and triple trailer rigs be on busy intercity routes?
cards.back: On busy intercity routes, double and triple trailer rigs can run longer than one hundred feet.

cards.front: Where should you avoid pulling in or moving over around a large vehicle?
cards.back: Do not pull onto a road in front of a large vehicle, and avoid moving over in front of one when you are about to turn off the road.

cards.front: What does it mean if you cannot see a truck driver in the truck's mirrors?
cards.back: If you cannot see a truck or bus driver in that vehicle's rearview mirrors, the driver cannot see you either.

cards.front: What is the No-Zone around a truck or bus?
cards.back: The No-Zone is the set of blind spots beside, behind and in front of a truck or bus where a car disappears from view, so stay out of it unless it is truly necessary.

cards.front: What should you avoid doing beside and behind a large vehicle?
cards.back: Do not ride alongside a large vehicle for long stretches, and do not tailgate one; keep a safety cushion around it.

cards.front: After passing a truck, when may you move back in, and what then?
cards.back: After passing a truck, wait until you can see its cab in your rearview mirror before moving back in, then signal, hold your speed and do not slow down ahead of it.

decks.domain: Missouri sharing the road: motorcycles, large trucks, pedestrians, bicycles, mopeds, electric bicycles, funeral processions, road rage, drunk drivers and littering

cards.front: Which lane should you avoid on steep grades and near weigh stations?
cards.back: On steep grades, keep out of the right lane of a divided or multi-lane road where slow trucks travel, and avoid the right lane near weigh stations so trucks can merge back in.

cards.front: Where must vehicles hauling hazardous materials stop?
cards.back: Vehicles hauling hazardous materials are required to stop at every railroad crossing, so be ready for them to stop.

cards.front: Why should you watch a truck's turn signal before passing it near a corner?
cards.back: A large truck may swing left first to make a right turn, so watch its turn signal before you try to pass it.

cards.front: How do car and loaded truck stopping distances compare at fifty-five miles per hour?
cards.back: At fifty-five miles per hour an average car stops in roughly one hundred thirty to one hundred forty feet, while a fully loaded tractor-trailer may need almost four hundred feet.

cards.front: How quickly does a loaded semi speed up?
cards.back: A loaded semi speeds up slowly: it may shift through ten gears to reach the limit, and its engine moves thirty to forty times the weight a car engine does.

cards.front: What should you do instead of cutting off a truck?
cards.back: Rather than cut off a truck, slow down and make your turn or lane change behind it, which costs only a few seconds.

cards.front: Why do car drivers misjudge trucks at intersections?
cards.back: A tractor-trailer often seems slower than it really is because of its size, which leads to crashes at intersections when car drivers misjudge its distance or speed.

decks.domain: Missouri sharing the road: motorcycles, large trucks, pedestrians, bicycles, mopeds, electric bicycles, funeral processions, road rage, drunk drivers and littering

cards.front: What should a pedestrian facing a Walk signal do before crossing?
cards.back: A pedestrian facing a Walk signal or green light has the right-of-way but should start across only after making sure drivers see them and stop.

cards.front: When should a pedestrian not start crossing, and who may finish?
cards.back: A pedestrian should not start crossing on a Don't Walk signal or a red or yellow light, but someone already in the street when the Don't Walk begins flashing may finish crossing.

cards.front: Where should pedestrians cross in business districts, and what if they cross mid-block?
cards.back: Pedestrians should use an intersection or crosswalk in a business district or between two close signalized intersections, and must yield to all traffic when crossing mid-block.

cards.front: Where there is no sidewalk, which side of the road should you walk on?
cards.back: Where there is no sidewalk, walk on the side of the road facing oncoming traffic.

cards.front: Should a pedestrian stand in a traffic lane to talk to a driver?
cards.back: A pedestrian should not stand in a traffic lane talking to a driver, but should wait for the car to park safely and stay on its curb side.

cards.front: Do you still yield to pedestrians when you have a green light?
cards.back: Even on a green light, a driver must yield to every pedestrian in the intersection, and must take care to avoid pedestrians whether or not they are obeying the law.

cards.front: May you pass a vehicle that has stopped for a pedestrian?
cards.back: Never pass a vehicle that has stopped or slowed for a pedestrian.

cards.front: What must you do in a school zone and at a crossing patrol?
cards.back: Obey the lower school-zone speed limit when its lights flash or children are present, and stop if a school crossing patrol member signals you.

cards.front: What must you do when a pedestrian with a guide dog or white cane is crossing?
cards.back: Always yield to a blind pedestrian; when someone crosses with a guide dog or a white cane, with or without a red tip, vehicles must stop completely.

cards.front: When must you yield to a pedestrian in a crosswalk?
cards.back: Yield to a pedestrian in a marked or unmarked crosswalk who is on your side of the road or approaching it.

cards.front: What should you avoid while waiting at a red signal near a crosswalk?
cards.back: Do not block the crosswalk while waiting at a red signal, and yield to pedestrians before driving across a sidewalk or crosswalk.

cards.front: How fast should you drive on residential streets lined with parked cars?
cards.back: On residential streets with parked cars, keep at or under the speed limit, adjusting to how far ahead you can see.

cards.front: When getting ready to turn right, especially on red, what should you watch for?
cards.back: When getting ready to turn right, especially on a red light, watch for pedestrians and cyclists coming up on your right.

decks.domain: Missouri sharing the road: motorcycles, large trucks, pedestrians, bicycles, mopeds, electric bicycles, funeral processions, road rage, drunk drivers and littering

cards.front: Where do most crashes with bicycles and mopeds happen?
cards.back: Most crashes with bicycles and mopeds happen at intersections, so scan for them and give them the same consideration as any other vehicle.

cards.front: Before turning right onto a main road, why look right as well as left?
cards.back: Before turning right onto a main road, look right as well as left for wrong-way cyclists on the road or the sidewalk.

cards.front: How do you turn right when a cyclist is ahead of you?
cards.back: If you need to turn right while following a cyclist, slow down and stay behind the rider until you can turn.

cards.front: When turning left, when must you yield to an oncoming cyclist?
cards.back: When turning left, yield to an oncoming cyclist unless you are certain you can finish the turn before the rider reaches the intersection.

cards.front: How much room do you give a bicycle or moped when passing?
cards.back: Give a bicycle or moped a full lane width when passing, slowing down if needed, and wait for a clear stretch if the lane is too narrow to share.

cards.front: What is a bicycle lane, and when may you cross it?
cards.back: A bicycle lane is a striped part of the roadway for bicycles; you may cross it to turn or to enter or leave the road, but you must yield to cyclists in it.

cards.front: What should you check before opening a car door into a traffic or bike lane?
cards.back: Look for passing cyclists before you open a car door into a traffic lane or bike lane.

cards.front: What rights and duties do moped and bicycle riders have, and which way must they ride?
cards.back: Moped and bicycle riders have the same rights and duties as motorists on public roads and must always ride with traffic, never against it.

cards.front: Where does a rider going slower than traffic ride, and when may the rider move left?
cards.back: A rider going slower than traffic generally keeps as far right as is safe, but may move toward the middle or left to turn left, avoid hazards, use a lane too narrow to share, or go straight past a right-turn-only lane.

cards.front: Why should riders leave room between themselves and the right edge of the road?
cards.back: The right edge of a road often holds ditches, gutters, sand and gravel shoulders, so riders should leave room between themselves and those hazards.

cards.front: On a one-way street, how far left may a cyclist ride?
cards.back: On a one-way street a bicyclist may ride as far left as is safe, and riders should check traffic and signal before shifting lanes or position.

cards.front: What may a less experienced cyclist do in heavy traffic?
cards.back: In heavy traffic, a less experienced cyclist may find it easier to wait near the curb until a safe gap opens.

cards.front: For teen and adult cyclists, is the street or the sidewalk safer?
cards.back: For teen and adult cyclists, riding in the street with traffic is far safer than riding on the sidewalk.

decks.domain: Missouri sharing the road: motorcycles, large trucks, pedestrians, bicycles, mopeds, electric bicycles, funeral processions, road rage, drunk drivers and littering

cards.front: May mopeds use the federal interstate highway system?
cards.back: Mopeds are not allowed on any part of the federal interstate highway system.

cards.front: What is needed to drive a moped on public streets?
cards.back: Driving a moped on public streets requires a valid driver license.

cards.front: Does Missouri require moped or bicycle riders to wear a helmet?
cards.back: Missouri does not require moped or bicycle riders to wear a helmet, although a safety-certified one can prevent serious head injury or death.

cards.front: Is a safety-certified helmet a legal requirement for moped and bicycle riders?
cards.back: For moped and bicycle riders a safety-certified helmet is advice, not a legal requirement, since state law does not demand one.

cards.front: How much space should a rider leave when passing to the left of a vehicle?
cards.back: Riders passing to the left of a parked or moving vehicle should leave three to four feet of space for a door that swings open or a car that swerves.

cards.front: Must mopeds and bicycles be registered or inspected, and what equipment, such as brakes, do they need?
cards.back: Missouri does not require mopeds or bicycles to be registered or inspected, but it does require certain equipment.

cards.front: What front light does a bicycle need at night, and how far must it show?
cards.back: From half an hour after sunset until half an hour before sunrise a bicycle needs a white front light that drivers can see from five hundred feet.

cards.front: What rear reflector or light does a bicycle need, and how far must it show?
cards.back: A rear red reflector must be at least two square inches, or a rear red light may be used instead, and drivers must be able to see it in their low beams from six hundred feet.

cards.front: How far must pedal or leg reflectors show in low beams?
cards.back: Reflectors or lights worn on the rider's shoes or lower legs, or fitted to the pedals or crank arms, must show in low beams at two hundred feet.

cards.front: How far must side reflectors or lights show, and what is exempt?
cards.back: Reflective material or lights on each side of the bicycle or rider must show in low beams at three hundred feet, a rule that does not cover mopeds meeting federal NHTSA standards.

cards.front: How do the bicycle lighting distances differ by item?
cards.back: The bicycle lighting distances differ by item: the white front light must be visible from five hundred feet, a rear red light or reflector shows at six hundred feet in low beams, side reflectors or lights at three hundred feet, and pedal or leg reflectors at two hundred feet.

cards.front: When do bicycle and car crashes climb, and what prevents most of them?
cards.back: Crashes between bicycles and cars climb sharply between sunset and sunrise, and proper lights and reflectors can prevent almost all of them.

decks.domain: Missouri sharing the road: motorcycles, large trucks, pedestrians, bicycles, mopeds, electric bicycles, funeral processions, road rage, drunk drivers and littering

cards.front: Does riding an electric bicycle that meets the state definition require a license?
cards.back: Riding an electric bicycle that meets the state definition does not require an operator license or a motorcycle license.

cards.front: What makes a device an electric bicycle under the state definition, and how do its classes work?
cards.back: Under the state definition an electric bicycle has working pedals, a seat or saddle, and an electric motor under seven hundred fifty watts.

cards.front: What makes a device a motorized bicycle, such as a moped?
cards.back: A motorized bicycle, such as a moped, has two or three wheels, an automatic transmission and a motor of no more than fifty cubic centimeters producing under three gross brake horsepower.

cards.front: What is the top speed for a device to count as a motorized bicycle?
cards.back: To count as a motorized bicycle, the device can go no faster than thirty miles per hour on level ground.

decks.domain: Missouri sharing the road: motorcycles, large trucks, pedestrians, bicycles, mopeds, electric bicycles, funeral processions, road rage, drunk drivers and littering

cards.front: How do vehicles in a funeral procession drive?
cards.back: Every vehicle in a funeral procession uses its flashing emergency lights and follows the car ahead as closely as is safe.

cards.front: When does an organized funeral procession have the right-of-way?
cards.back: An organized funeral procession has the right-of-way at every intersection regardless of traffic signals, except for emergency vehicles or when police direct otherwise.

cards.front: What may drivers outside a funeral procession not do?
cards.back: Drivers outside a funeral procession may not cut between its moving vehicles, join it to get the right-of-way, or pass its vehicles except in a lane provided for passing.

cards.front: When may a driver outside a procession enter the intersection it is crossing on red?
cards.back: A driver not in a funeral procession may enter an intersection the procession is crossing on a red light only without crossing the procession's path.

cards.front: What is road rage?
cards.back: Road rage is an uncontrolled display of anger by a driver, usually in response to another driver, that can damage property or injure people.

cards.front: Name some examples of road-rage behavior.
cards.back: Examples of road-rage behavior include honking, flashing headlights, tailgating, chasing another car, aggressive gestures, sudden braking, deliberate blocking, cutting off and assault.

cards.front: Can road rage habits be unlearned?
cards.back: Road rage habits can be unlearned, but doing so takes self-discipline from the driver.

cards.front: How should you respond to road rage, and how do you report it safely?
cards.back: Faced with road rage, stay calm and do not respond in kind, note the location and descriptions of the driver and vehicle, and report it to local authorities as soon as you can.

cards.front: What should you do if you think you have seen a drunk driver?
cards.back: If you think you have seen a drunk driver, tell the police at once and give the plate number, a description of the car and driver, and its location.

cards.front: What penalties can a court impose for littering?
cards.back: Littering is illegal, and a court can impose a fine of up to one thousand dollars, up to one year in jail, or both.

cards.front: Why is tossing a lit cigarette from a car dangerous?
cards.back: A lit cigarette tossed from a car window can blow into the vehicle behind and cause damage or injury, which is one reason littering is illegal.

recap_hooks.text: Motorcycles are easy to miss and hard to judge, so riders should not count on the right-of-way.
Never share a lane with a motorcycle, and give it a full lane when passing.
Riders need a helmet and the right license, and bright clothing, lights and signals help them be seen.
Trucks are huge and long, so never cut in front of one or linger in its No-Zone.
If you cannot see the driver in the mirror, the driver cannot see you; after passing, wait to see the cab before moving back.
Trucks swing wide to turn, stop in far more distance than cars and speed up slowly.
Leave the right lane on grades and near weigh stations, expect hazmat stops at crossings, and turn behind a truck.
Pedestrians cross on Walk only after drivers see them, use crosswalks in town and walk facing traffic.
Drivers yield to pedestrians even on green, never pass a stopped car, and stop fully for a white cane or guide dog.
Slow in school zones and residential streets, keep crosswalks clear and check right before turning right.
Most bike crashes happen at intersections, so look both ways, stay behind cyclists to turn and yield when turning left.
Give bikes a full lane to pass, yield in bike lanes and look before opening doors.
Riders follow the same rules, ride with traffic and keep right except where the guide allows moving left.
Mopeds stay off interstates and need a license, and helmets are advice rather than law for mopeds and bikes.
Bikes need good brakes and lights: front at five hundred feet, rear at six hundred, sides at three hundred, pedals at two hundred.
Riders leave three to four feet beside vehicles, and good lighting prevents most night crashes.
An electric bicycle with pedals, a seat and a small motor needs no license.
Classes one and three assist only while pedaling, and class two runs on the motor alone.
A motorized bicycle like a moped has a small automatic engine and tops out at thirty miles per hour.
Funeral processions keep flashers on and go through intersections, and others may not cut in or cross their path.
Meet road rage with calm, note the details, pull off and report it, and report suspected drunk drivers too.
Littering, including tossed cigarettes, is illegal and can bring a fine, jail or both.

sec05-R06 and sec05-R07 carry the bare unit abbreviation mph in their accepted wording, which fails the spoken-form card gate; the three electric bicycle classes are taught on the sec05-R08 electric bicycle definition card, in that card's script, the module lesson and their own exam items.

sec05-F50's accepted wording contains a star symbol in the dialing code, which fails the spoken-form card gate; reporting road rage by phone after leaving the road is taught on the sec05-F49 road rage response card, in that card's script, the module lesson and its own exam item.
